Foreordained
fōr-ŏr-dānd´
v. (appointed beforehand; of Christ, appointed before the world was)
From fore- + ordain, Latin ordinare, to set in order. Peter's Greek is proginosko in its full covenantal sense — foreknown, which in Hebraic usage means chosen and set apart beforehand, not merely observed in advance.

Biblical Definition

Peter grounds the redemption of sinners in an appointment older than the creation: “Who verily was foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifest in these last times for you” (1 Peter 1:20). The Lamb was not an answer improvised after the fall; He was appointed before there was a world to fall. The verse before names the price: “But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:19). The same epistle opens by putting the church in the same decree: “Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied” (1 Peter 1:2). Paul locates the choosing at the identical point on the calendar and gives its end: “According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love” (Ephesians 1:4). Note in him. Election is never a bare selection of individuals; it is a choosing of a people in a Head who was Himself foreordained. The decree and the cross are one plan, and neither is a contingency.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines foreordain as to ordain or appoint beforehand; to predetermine.

expand to see more

FOREORDAIN, v.t. To ordain or appoint beforehand; to predetermine; to predestinate.

FOREORDINATION, n. Previous ordination or appointment; predetermination; predestination.

ORDAIN, v.t. [L. ordino, from ordo, order.] To set; to establish; to institute; to constitute; to appoint.

DECREE, n. In theology, predetermined purpose of God; the purpose or determination of an immutable Being.

ELECT, v.t. [L. electus, from eligo, to choose.] In theology, to designate, choose or select as an object of mercy or favor.

Key Scripture

1 Peter 1:20 — "Who verily was foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifest in these last times for you,"

1 Peter 1:19 — "But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:"

1 Peter 1:2 — "Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied."

Ephesians 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:"

Modern Corruption

Foreordination is reduced to foresight — God looking down the corridor of time to see who would choose Him — which makes the decree a report rather than a determination.

expand to see more

The prescient view holds that God foreknew who would believe and elected them on that basis. It cannot be got out of 1 Peter 1:20, where the object of the same verb is Christ Himself. No one supposes the Father looked ahead, observed that the Son would volunteer, and ratified it. The word means appointed beforehand, and it means the same thing of the Lamb and of the people the Lamb was appointed to redeem. Foreknowledge in Hebraic usage is covenantal knowing — you only have I known of all the families of the earth — not advance information.

Ephesians 1:4 closes the other escape. The choosing is before the foundation of the world, which is before any creature exists to be foreseen doing anything; and its purpose is that we should be holy, which makes holiness the fruit of election rather than its cause. Conditional election reverses both the timing and the direction. The 1689 confesses that God ordained whatsoever comes to pass, yet so that neither is God the author of sin nor is violence offered to the will of the creature — a doctrine that grants the mystery and refuses to resolve it by shrinking the decree.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek proginosko (G4267), to know beforehand, foreordain; prognosis (G4268), foreknowledge; eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; proorizo (G4309), to predestinate.

expand to see more

Greek proginosko (G4267) — to foreknow, foreordain; 1 Peter 1:20, of Christ Himself.

Greek prognosis (G4268) — foreknowledge; 1 Peter 1:2 and Acts 2:23, the determinate counsel.

Greek proorizo (G4309) — to mark out beforehand; Romans 8:29 and Ephesians 1:5.

Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out for oneself; Ephesians 1:4, chosen in him.

Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; Amos 3:2, covenantal knowing, not information.

Usage

"“Foreordained before the foundation of the world” — and the object is Christ."

"“Manifest in these last times for you” — the decree kept its appointment."

"“Chosen us in him” — never a bare selection; always in a Head."
